processing: Orthodox Darjeeling black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and fired, with lighter oxidation in spring and fuller oxidation in summer, as is usual for the district. The garden is listed as organic.
harvest_season: As across Darjeeling, first flush in spring, second flush in early summer, then monsoon and autumn pickings; the first two usually fetch the most attention.
appearance_dry: Typical of Darjeeling leaf, a mix of olive-green and brown twists with pale tips, darker in the later flushes.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in spring lots, clear amber in summer and autumn lots.
appearance_wet: Tender green-and-copper leaf in spring, more uniformly brown later in the year.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about this garden's own cup. Darjeelings of this type are floral and brisk in spring, fruitier and rounder in summer.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Drop to about 85°C for first flush; pull it early if it starts to grip.

vintage_note: Like other Darjeeling estate teas, it is sold by year and flush, often with an invoice or lot number and a leaf grade. First flush is at its best within about a year of picking. A named flush and year tells you far more than a generic Darjeeling label.
description:
Tumsong is a Darjeeling garden and a village of the same name, in the Jorebunglow Sukhiapokhri block, spread over a very wide altitude range of 2,700 to 5,500 feet. It has 114 hectares under tea out of 186 in total.

It is part of the Chamong Group, a large producer of organic Darjeeling, and appears on lists of organic gardens. Processing follows the usual orthodox Darjeeling pattern, with light oxidation in spring and more in summer.

There is little published about what sets Tumsong's cup apart, so treat it as you would other Darjeelings: expect flowers and briskness in first flush, ripe fruit in second, and brew spring lots a little cooler.

Buy it by year and flush. If you find a lot, compare it with another Chamong Group garden from the same season to see what the place itself brings.
history:
Tea planting at Tumsong began in 1867 under J.A. Wernicke, who also started the plantation at nearby Lingia. It began small, with a 200-acre garden, and grew from there.

The bushes were planted around a hillside temple to the goddess Tamsa Devi, and local people kept the right to come and worship there. The garden now belongs to the Chamong Group.
